name: Boscombe Surf Reef
year: Construction began June 2008; officially opened 19 November 2009 [R1][R4]. Primary-source timeline (Rendle 2016 p. 64): construction started 30 Aug 2008, suspended 13 Nov 2008, resumed 18 Apr 2009, official opening 2 Oct 2009 (the text on p. 65 says completion Nov 2009 after 18 months) [R17].
type: Submerged multi-purpose artificial surf reef built from large sand-filled geotextile containers ("geobags"), not rock [R1][R4][R7].
purpose: Coastal-town regeneration and surf tourism: create a reliable, higher-quality wave to roughly double good surfing days (from ~77 to ~154/yr) and double annual surf-related beach visits (from ~5,000 to ~10,000); marketed as Europe's/the Northern Hemisphere's first artificial surf reef [R1][R3][R4].
size: ~55 geotextile containers, each ~2–3 m high and ~60 m long; total sand-fill volume ≈13,000 m³; footprint ≈1 hectare (2.5 acres); positioned 220 m from the seawall base, ~240 m east of the pier [R4][R7]. Rendle's thesis (primary): 32 containers built in two layers, placed by divers and filled in situ (p. 68); design drawing of Dec 2006 shows about 46 labelled bags, footprint 4,474 m2, bag volume 10,450 m3 + fill 1,750 m3 (Fig. 5.3, p. 95); Table 4.4 design: volume 11,900 m3, footprint 5,450 m2, length 120 m, height 2.8-4.1 m (p. 70); containers up to 67 m long, 100-800 m3 (p. 69); eight T4 containers about 4 m diameter, 65-70 m long, 746.7 m3 each (Table 5.3, p. 98; p. 121). Counts differ between sources (32 / about 46 / 54-55) [R17]. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4) give 12,800 m3 [R18] (the designers' value; Blacka Table 4.4 cost/rate implies about 12,760 m3 [R19]); volume sources therefore disagree: about 13,000 [R4][R7] / 11,900 or 12,200 (Rendle design) / 12,800 [R18], all kept. Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.2 p.66): footprint 80 m (longshore) x 90 m (cross-shore), depth 3-5 m, 225 m offshore, submergence 0.5 m, tide range 1.8 m, T~4 s, H~0.5 m (Table 4.3) [R19]; the card's 120 m length is Rendle's design figure, so footprint figures differ by source. Project-traced outline (not a source statement): reef plan area 4,042 m2, minimum rotated rectangle 121.1 x 45.0 m, about 220-225 m offshore, west edge 242 m east of the pier head, traced on the Esri Wayback image of 2011-09-28 and checked against the April 2011 survey figure [R22][R21]. The '1 hectare' of [R4]/Wikipedia is therefore not the plan area of the reef body (4,042 m2); the basis of the 1 ha figure is not stated by those sources (not reconciled).
cost: £3–3.2 million actually spent on the reef structure itself, against an original 1999–2003-era estimate of £1.4 million; the wider Boscombe seafront/pier regeneration scheme (reef + pier refurbishment + seafront) totalled ≈£11 million [R1][R2]. One New Zealand outlet states the cost as "more than NZD $6 million," over a year behind schedule — not corroborated by any UK source [R8]. Rendle (2016, p. 65-67): original GBP 600,000 (Black et al. 2000), GBP 1.1 m (ASR Ltd 2006, incl. 20 % contingency), final about GBP 3.2 m; repairs and marine-park works a further GBP 700,000 (funded partly by GBP 306,531 insurance and a GBP 254,000 Coastal Communities Fund grant, p. 64); Weight (2000) estimate GBP 618,000 for two reefs (Table 4.3, p. 66) [R17]. Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.4): about A$4.9 M in 2013 dollars, A$384 per m3 [R19]. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4) note the contract was fixed-price, so claimed overruns concern delays rather than contract cost [R18]; this can sit beside the early-estimate comparison above.
cost_usd_approx: £3.2M ≈ US $5.1M at 2009 average GBP/USD rates (~1.59); NZD $6M ≈ US $4.2M at 2010 average NZD/USD rates (~0.70) — rough conversions, not sourced from any single article [R1][R2][R8]. ASSUMPTION: the exchange rates (GBP/USD ~1.59, NZD/USD ~0.70) are unsourced estimates of this project (not confirmed against a rate table); order of magnitude only.
financed_by: Bournemouth Borough Council, funded via sale of a car park (on which Barratt Developments built the Honeycombe Chine Flats) and sale of beach "pods" as part of the Overstrand seafront building [R1][R4].
motivation: Boscombe was a rundown 20th-century seaside suburb of Bournemouth in need of regeneration; the reef was one plank of a wider council-led seafront renewal that also refurbished Boscombe Pier and built new beachfront "pods" and flats [R1][R10]. A feasibility study was approved in 1999 and detailed plans approved in March 2003, with construction not starting until 2008 [R6][R1]. Financing was structured opportunistically around unrelated seafront property sales rather than a dedicated capital grant [R1][R4].
designer: Dr Kerry Black (oceanographer, ex-University of Waikato/NIWA, co-founder of ASR Ltd) did the wave-science/concept design; Shaw Mead (ASR co-founder) is credited as design/surf-science lead [R8][R7].
contractor: ASR Ltd (Artificial Surf Reefs Ltd), a New Zealand company; managing director Nick Behunin [R1][R4][R6].
status_now: Permanently closed to surfing since 31 March/April 2011 after storm and boat-propeller damage; ASR Ltd went into liquidation September 2012; rebranded and reopened in stages (2014, then 2017) as a "Coastal Activity Park" for diving, snorkelling, windsurfing/kitesurfing and other non-surf water activities; by 2018 described as largely forgotten/neglected; debris from the structure was still washing ashore as late as Boxing Day 2017 [R1][R3][R4][R8].
hover_text: A ~1-hectare, 13,000 m³ sand-filled geotextile-bag surf reef opened November 2009 for £3–3.2M (Bournemouth Borough Council, funded via land/beach-pod sales); a boat-propeller strike and storm damage forced permanent closure to surfing by 2011, ASR Ltd liquidated in 2012, and the site was rebranded a non-surf "Coastal Activity Park" from 2014 [R1][R2][R4][R8].
design_as_planned: The reef was designed as a submerged, angled ramp of stacked geotextile sand containers that would intercept the dominant swell direction and reshape it into rideable peeling waves, rather than "creating" waves from nothing. ASR director Shaw Mead described the mechanism directly: "The reef doesn't actually create waves. It's angled to catch the mean wave direction, and it acts as a ramp which changes the way the waves break" [R10]. The design target was a "Grade 5" wave under good swell conditions, producing rides of roughly 75 m to the right and 35 m to the left, suited to bodyboarders and surfers [R10]. Eleven specific design/performance objectives were set, including materially increasing surf-day frequency (from ~77 to ~154 good surf days/yr) and beach-visit numbers (from ~5,000 to ~10,000/yr) [R1][R2].
as_built_vs_design: The structure eventually installed — 55 sand-filled geotextile bags forming a ~1-hectare submerged mound ~13,000 m³ in volume — matched the general geotube concept, but construction ran roughly a decade behind the original 1999–2003 planning timeline and cost more than double the original £1.4 million estimate, landing at £3–3.2 million for the reef alone [R1][R2][R6]. Construction was repeatedly delayed and beset by "setbacks during building works" before the reef finally opened in November 2009 [R1]. Shaw Mead later blamed the outcome on "wrangling over funds, political in-fighting and bad project management decisions," distancing his own design/surf-science role from those problems [R8]. Rendle (2016): built crest about +0.5 m chart datum against a design crest of 0 m CD (Table 4.4; 0.3 m CD on the Dec 2006 drawing), so the crest is higher than planned (p. 70); not all containers were filled to capacity and some bags of the plan were missing in the final construction (p. 98, p. 122) [R17]. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4): the reef was built to design under a fixed-price contract and completed in late September 2009 [R18] (designers' view; the card's headline opening date is November 2009 and Rendle 2016 documents shortfalls [R17], so sources disagree). AUDIT NOTE 2026-10-10: 'submerged' holds at high water only; the built crest (+0.5 m CD, about -0.9 m MSL using the project's conversion MSL = CD - 1.40 m, NTSLF offset; Rendle uses 1.66 m, unresolved) is exposed at low tide (Rendle p.70-71) [R17][R20].
outcome: A University of Plymouth interim evaluation (Dr Mark Davidson, published May 2010) found the reef met only 4 of its 11 original design objectives, stating: "The wave length is rather too intense and challenging [and it] is not quite as consistent as it should be" [R1][R2]. This evaluation is credited solely to Dr Mark Davidson in every source found; a claim (raised during a Gemini-survey cross-check) that the evaluation was co-authored by "Reeve" and "Medina" is not confirmed anywhere and is rejected — the only genuine Davidson co-authored paper found online is the separate, later Rendle & Davidson (2012, ICCE Proceedings) study on structural degradation, with a different co-author [R1]. In practice the reef worked best around low tide, with rides largely limited to steep, short sections, mainly ridden by bodyboarders rather than the standup surfers it was marketed to [R1]. A routine inspection in March 2011 found "substantial changes" to the reef's profile; it was closed for safety on 31 March 2011 [R1]. In April 2011 further damage was found, with one geo-container removed and another repaired, apparently after an unidentified boat's propeller struck the reef [R1][R9]. Repairs begun in August 2011 were suspended for winter and never satisfactorily completed [R1][R7]. ASR Ltd went into liquidation in September 2012 (one source: November 2012), owing the council roughly £14,800–£15,000; the council obtained a £306,531 insurance settlement in 2013 [R1][R4][R6]. A 2012 plan to repurpose the site as a dive/snorkel trail was itself abandoned [R5]. The site was rebranded in 2014 and again in 2017 as a "Coastal Activity Park," with surfing dropped as a priority [R1][R6]. Debris from the decaying structure was reported washing ashore as late as Boxing Day 2017 [R8]. Rendle (2016, p. 70-71): Davidson 2010 found 4 of 11 criteria met and 2 partly; rides about 20 m left / 40 m right against 20 m / 65 m designed; surfable only 1-2 h around mid-tide because the crest is exposed at low tide and too deep at high tide; the wave model shows attenuation in the lee (p. 143-144) and the shoreline did not respond, no salient (p. 102) [R17]. SOURCES DISAGREE on the Plymouth evaluation score: Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4), reporting the Plymouth University monitoring of May 2010, say the reef met 7 of 11 criteria (7 of the 9 agreed by Council and builders) and that media mis-reported '4 out of 10' [R18]; Rendle (2016, p.70-71) gives 4 of 11 met and 2 partly [R17]. The authors of [R18] designed the reef (interested party); Davidson (2010) must be checked directly. Both kept. Shoreline: Blacka et al. (2013, p.70) report no noticeable long-term change of the 0 m shoreline (Rendle & Davidson 2012); design accretion was predicted mostly near the -1 m contour (K. Black pers. comm.), which Rendle & Davidson did not report; inshore scour and steepening were well predicted; rated surfing 'partially', protection 'minor' [R19].
why_worked_or_failed: Shaw Mead's own later analysis concluded sand-filled geotextile bags were a structural dead end: "the sandbags were an evolutionary dead-end," and "as soon as even a single sand-filled container broke and lost sand, the whole structure changed shape due to the fluid nature of sand" — a design fundamentally vulnerable to point-impact damage [R8][R9]. The proximate damage cause was a boat-propeller strike, a mechanism Geosynthetics Magazine groups with damage at other ASR reefs elsewhere (anchor damage at Gold Coast, debris strikes at Kovalam, over-filling at Mount Maunganui) as evidence of a general geotextile-reef vulnerability pattern [R9]. Even before the propeller strike, the University of Plymouth's Davidson evaluation had already found the reef meeting only 4 of 11 design objectives, indicating the wave-shaping design itself, not only later physical damage, fell short [R1][R2]. Shaw Mead's own explanation for the broader project's failure also emphasises non-engineering causes — "wrangling over funds, political in-fighting and bad project management decisions" during a near-decade gap between 2003 planning approval and 2008 construction start [R8][R6][R1]. Rendle (2016): after winter 2009-10 sand moved inside the bags (seaward to landward, p. 94); a T4 container (746.7 m3) lost its sand in 2011 (cause contested: weak container, propeller strike or vandalism) and a second in 2012, together 1,493.4 m3 = 12.5 % of 11,900 m3 (Table 5.3, p. 98), gaps of 5 m then 8-10 m, 2 m crest dip; construction shortcuts (wrong grain size supplied, weather, end-of-summer deadline, p. 98); first inspection found poorly repaired tears (p. 120) [R17]. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4-5): 17 bathymetry surveys and 3 beach-profile surveys; beach accreted up to 60 m over >500 m within 6 months; about 60 hardwood groynes in Poole Bay (roughly every 180 m) and renourishment every 10-12 years, so the beach response sits within a managed shoreline [R18].
unexpected_results: The project drew media coverage in an estimated 60 countries around its 2009 opening, and local Boscombe hospitality businesses reported a real economic uplift regardless of the reef's technical shortcomings [R2]. Some media coverage carried headlines setting expectations the reef's actual short, steep, low-tide-only wave could not meet [R9]. The site was closed in 2011 over safety concerns involving hazardous undercurrents and gaps in the deteriorating structure, serious enough that local surfer/photographer Chris Skone-Roberts warned "it is just a question of time before someone dies" [R2]. Loose material and debris from the decaying geotextile bags continued washing ashore for years after closure, documented as late as Boxing Day 2017 [R8]. Dolphins were reported investigating the new structure shortly after construction, an unplanned/unmeasured ecological footnote [R10].
could_be_better: Shaw Mead (ASR co-designer) concluded the material choice itself was wrong — sand-filled geotextile bags are "an evolutionary dead-end" for a structure that must survive years of surf-zone wave energy and occasional impacts — and moved ASR's subsequent multi-purpose-reef designs to rock construction instead [R8]. Geosynthetics Magazine's review implies the fix is structural redundancy: a single ruptured bag should not be able to reshape the whole reef, pointing toward either more failure-tolerant bag engineering or abandoning fabric containers for point-impact-prone sites like a boat channel [R9]. The University of Plymouth's own evaluation implies the wave-shaping geometry needed further hydrodynamic refinement even independent of material failure, since only 4 of 11 objectives were met while the structure was still intact [R1][R2]. Local critics, including councillor Ben Grower, framed the entire project as a governance and money failure rather than a fixable engineering detail [R2][R5]. Rendle's lessons (p. 121-122): compare real seabed level with the design before building, no bags missing from the final build, seal the fill ports, the +0.5 m higher crest added stress, avoid geotextile in an exposed shallow surf zone [R17].
relevance_to_israel: Boscombe's tidal range is modest by UK Atlantic-coast standards (same-day check showed roughly 0.9–1.1 m high-to-low, illustrative only) [R12]; Haifa's Mediterranean coast is effectively micro-tidal, though no sourced numeric tidal-range figure for Haifa was found in this research [R14]. What transfers directly: Boscombe's central lesson is that geotextile-sandbag construction is vulnerable to point-impact damage (boat strikes, anchors, debris) and to cascading shape-change once any single bag ruptures, regardless of tidal regime [R8][R9]. Haifa's proposed reef site is assessed against real Shikmona-buoy wave data (significant wave height 0.45–0.8 m in the surfable window, occasional peaks to ~1.2 m), a much gentler wave-energy environment than the UK Channel/Atlantic-influenced south coast that shaped Boscombe's design — meaning less storm-wave loading, but underscoring that any Israeli project should still plan explicitly for boat-strike/anchor exposure in a working coastal-shipping and fishing environment [R14]. Tide levels from the design paper (Mead et al. 2010, Table 1): MHWS +0.81 m and MLWS -0.95 m relative to MSL, i.e. a spring range of 1.76 m [R20] (project conversion from chart datum; the same-day 0.9-1.1 m above is one day only). Haifa wave figures [R14] are Lior's own readings of the IsraMar Shikmona buoy, not a published source.

hero_recommendation.reason: Best single image for a reader unfamiliar with the site: shows the pier, beach, town and the reef's rectangular submerged footprint all in one aerial frame at the correct scale and offshore distance, directly illustrating the dossier's stated size/position. Basis: closed to surfing since 31 March 2011 after the reef lost sand/changed shape [R1][R17]; Plymouth University evaluation met 4 of 11 objectives (Rendle p.70-71 [R17]; Mead & Borrero count 7 of 11 [R18], an interested party); ASR Ltd liquidated 2012 [R1]; rebranded as non-surf park [R1][R6]. Re-checked 2026-10-10; unchanged.
